System1 & Advertising Association’s November Ads of the Month

Once again, we’re looking at three great current ads which are effective on their own terms but also offer lessons to brands looking to incorporate sustainability messaging in their campaigns. This month the focus is on music, with three commercials that use it brilliantly to enhance storytelling and create a mood that makes their messaging stickier and more memorable. 

Deliveroo x Tesco – “Woohoo”

First up we have a 5-Star collaboration from Tesco and Deliveroo, celebrating the fact that these brands are teaming up – you can now access Tesco groceries on the Deliveroo app. The ad is an excellent example of turning what could be a dry bit of brand news into a hilarious, highly entertaining ad, and uses its soundtrack brilliantly. 

The ad stages a meeting between a Tesco and a Deliveroo worker who approach each other warily before breaking into a celebratory hug. Now firm friends, the two brand buddies embark on a series of delivery adventures to a swaggering 80s rock soundtrack from Kenny Loggins. The pair acting like movie stars to the music – and the reactions of others around them – is what makes the ad so funny. 

The ad scores an excellent 5.6-Stars on our Test Your Ad platform, predicting exceptional potential for long-term business impact and market share gain. There’s also a strong short-term Spike performance. In the “Reasons for Emotion” section we can see what a vital role the humour and the music is playing: “Funny ad, great music” and “a seriously funny ad while getting a message across” say two of the Happy viewers. 

There’s no explicit sustainability message in the Tesco x Deliveroo ad but it’s still a valuable lesson that if you have news or an initiative to announce you can make it funny or entertaining, and that creative use of the soundtrack can really enhance that response. 

Movember – “For the growers: It’s all coming back to me now” 

There’s more explicit social messaging in the epic ad from men’s health charity Movember, promoting its annual sponsored moustache-growing initiative. The ad follows one “Grower” from the painful decision to shave off his beard, across the weeks of growing his moustache, and to the acceptance and popularity that a full ‘tache brings him.  

It’s hilariously over the top, and the soundtrack is once again a big reason why. Celine Dion’s bombastic ballad “It’s All Coming Back to Me Now” plays across the whole 2½ minute ad and the action on screen tracks the melodrama of the song. It’s no wonder the ad ends up in the top 4% of all charity ads despite its length, scoring a very strong 4.5-Star Rating. The ad performs especially well with young viewers, who give it a maximum 5.9-Star score in our indicative demographic report. 

Humour and positivity tend to be winning tactics in the charity sector, and there’s a lot that sustainable advertising can learn from that. If you package a message in humour, then a commitment to behavioural change – like growing a ‘mo’ for a month – becomes a great deal easier. Here the genius choice of song is a key element in creating that sense of fun and drama.

M&S – “Scottish Haddock | Farm to Foodhall”

Finally let’s have a look at M&S, whose “Farm to Foodhall” ads we’ve talked about before. This one is another winner, with regular presenter Tom Kerridge hitching a ride on a salmon fishing boat and getting the lowdown on the crew’s commitment to sustainable fish farming. As usual, the naturalistic format and Kerridge’s friendly presence makes the sustainable message feel more human and credible. It’s a terrific example of what behavioural science calls “The Messenger Effect”, where who’s saying it is as important as what is being said. 

The ad scores a very strong 4.5-Star Rating but performs even better on the short-term Spike Rating and Brand Fluency (rapid and accurate recognition) measures, with an exceptional 95% of people recognising who the ad is for. And here’s where the soundtrack comes in. M&S have been using Fleetwood Mac’s instrumental classic “Albatross” since the beginning of the campaign, as an intro to each ad. It sets a restful tone which fits the naturalistic, conversational vibe of the commercials. In doing this they’ve turned the track into a distinctive brand asset, helping the very rapid brand recognition. 

The “Farm to Foodhall” series has a lot of positive sustainable messages, but their specifics may not be as important as the lesson of “Albatross”: consistency pays off. Build up a consistent style through visuals and music and your ads will be a lot more quickly recognisable, which lets you concentrate on the messaging and building audience trust. Whether it’s a one-off song or a consistent use like M&S, the choice of soundtrack can be a massive messaging assist. 

Create with Confidence®

Great advertising changes how people feel before it changes what they do.

Testing with real people helps you understand whether your creative is overcoming indifference, building emotional connection, and making your brand impossible to ignore. It shows whether you’re creating work that resonates instinctively, communicates clearly, and earns its place in memory.

Because effectiveness isn’t a matter of opinion. It’s measurable.

With System1’s creative testing solutions, you can optimise every campaign before launch, creating advertising that is more emotional, more distinctive, and more likely to drive long-term commercial growth.

Walkers Go for Gold With Premium Results

Walkers

Gold Range

4.6

Want to stay ahead of the latest winning innovation trends? Innovation of the Week, powered by System1’s Test Your Innovation testing, is your regular spotlight on the newest concepts hitting the market. Sign up to get it delivered straight to your inbox every week!

Speak to our innovation team today!

How do you approach innovation when you’re the market leader? The challenges for a leading brand in a category are specific ones – expanding your brand into new sectors, defending against challengers, creating more lifetime value from existing customers and all without cannibalising current sales. So this week’s Innovation Of The Week comes from Walkers, the long-term market leader in the UK’s crisp category, who are launching an entire new premium range, Walkers Gold.

Walkers already have an excellent track record in innovation. They helped launch the premium crisp category with Walkers Sensations, which specialised in new and vibrant flavours. Their limited edition crisp ranges and brand collaborations keep regular customers excited and drive social interest. But the Walkers Gold range is filling a different market niche, looking to take share from competitors Tyrells and Kettle Chips, whose pitch to consumers is upmarket flavours rather than novelties, an emphasis on provenance and a pack design that gives a sense of the artisanal.

Walkers’ own recent redesign puts an emphasis on heritage, with the signature of founder Henry Walker now added to packs. And the flavour range for Walkers Gold – classy, subtle flavours like Sea Salt And Olive Oil and Black Truffle – is clearly aimed at the sophisticated crisp buyer. So how do consumers react to the concept?

In our Test Your Innovation report there’s good news all round for Walkers – the Walkers Gold crisps are a 4.6-Star hit, a result predicting strong market success. The new range particularly shone in our “share trading game”, where we ask participants whether or not they’d buy shares in a new idea – getting a result distinct from their own emotional response to the line. Walkers Gold did exceptionally well here, with 76% opting to buy shares. That’s a sign that even if consumers aren’t interested in the line themselves, they recognise its strong commercial potential.

Walkers Gold also did well in terms of emotional response. 58% of people said the concept made them feel happy, versus the UK average of 36% for a new idea. Negative responses, meanwhile, were much lower than average: people don’t find the concept at all weird or offputting. The comments given as reasons for emotion show that people understand why Walkers are launching a new premium line. “It’s Walkers trying something new to compete with the Premium brand crisp ranges” said one participant. “The flavours make the product appealing and the packaging looks great” said another.

It’s also clear from the comments and the Implicit Attributes test (rapid associations of a product with attributes) that a lot of the appeal is in the Walkers brand itself. This is the central benefit of being a market leader: people like and trust you. The highest scores Walkers Gold received (90%+ for each) were for “Believable”, “Recognisable” and “Fits With The Brand”. But there were also scores well above the test average for “Premium”, “Relevant” and “Recommended” – consumers understand that these Walkers crisps are something out of the ordinary.

What the Test Your Innovation report is showing here is an excellent combination of results for a market leader looking to expand into a premium sector where challengers have set up shop. Walkers Gold has all the benefits of consistency and brand recognition, while also clearly creating an impression of something new and premium. The public understands the new line, and they like what they see.

Creative & Media Partnership Director, LATAM (renata.buess@system1research.com)

Published: 26 November 2026

Caloi Goes Back to the 1980s to Unlock the Power of Nostalgia

Caloi

Caloi. Infância - Convocação.

5.1
View in Portuguese

Don’t forget my… Nobody did. 

One of Brazil’s most iconic campaigns is back.

“Don’t forget my Caloi” became a meme before social media even existed, trending for years on end and becoming a neat way of reminding someone about anything at all.

In October this year, Caloi launched a film with a distinctly 1980s feel, made entirely of photographs and featuring an ending familiar to everyone who grew up renting VHS tapes: having to rewind the tape before returning it. And all this in a market where everyone is chasing the latest format and the platform of the moment.

In Test Your Ad Pro, the film achieved 79% Happiness, against a Brazilian average of 53%. Emotional Intensity was 2.49, against a norm of 1.96. It scored 5.1 Stars, indicating long-term growth potential, while Spike and Brand Fluency were also Exceptional. A rare triple crown.

Click here to see the full report

An ad that looks backwards has won on every front in an industry that is often fixated on the future, almost like a cult. The advertising world is obsessed with novelty: new campaigns, new positioning and new platforms. But often, the most effective advertising emerges when brands look to their legacy of campaigns and brand assets to revive earlier successes. Frequently, this involves reinventing them in new ways.

When the psychologist Daniel Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics, he brought forward evidence that the more we feel, the more we buy. That motto was, and still is, embraced by the most effective agencies and brands. We know that emotion sells and that nostalgia is a vehicle for it. But that’s not to say nostalgia-core is here to stay.

The children of the 1980s, now around 45, were the ones who wanted to leave the house and ride their bikes, feel the wind in their hair, meet their friends and set off on an adventure.

Forty years on, those children are parents, and some are even grandparents. The campaign makes an almost imperceptible shift: the line becomes “Don’t forget your child’s Caloi”. The Caloi ad now rewinds the tape but speaks to the adult rather than directly to the child. This keeps it, in principle, out of the more sensitive territory of advertising regulations. It’s an interesting angle: using nostalgia as a strategy to reach children through the adults who make purchasing decisions. The same message has a new recipient. The child who used to ask is now the adult who decides, and the consumer’s memory stops being merely a recollection and becomes a purchasing instruction for the next generation.

But what actually happens inside someone who remembers? I have covered this in another analysis, but there is more research worth exploring, which the strategist Richard Shotton also frequently references. Jannine Lasaleta, Constantine Sedikides and Kathleen Vohs conducted six experiments published in the Journal of Consumer Research. Participants placed in a nostalgic state were willing to pay more for products, spent more money (but not more time) and placed less value on money. The authors’ explanation: nostalgia weakens the desire for money because it creates a feeling of social connection.

Looking at the Test Your Ad results for Caloi, we can see that nostalgia takes people back to a time when their decisions were based less on price and more on feeling. The memory surrounds the consumer with loved ones, and the same familiar people, places and objects appear in almost everyone’s recollections: family, friends, the street and the bicycle. In the comments, people talk about their own childhood adventures and how children today need to play outdoors. The ad acts as a door, and each person walks through it to reach their own story.

It is worth heeding Byron Sharp’s caution: these experiments are laboratory-based and measure willingness to pay, not sales. It is a plausible and well-documented mechanism, not a promise of margin. But our test suggests that Caloi stands to reap the rewards, both now and in the future.

Here, though, I want to highlight the central idea of System1’s study, The Magic of Compound Creativity: creativity doesn’t add up, it accumulates. Every ad that uses the same assets, characters, tone and codes inherits the memory of those that came before it. Caloi has an asset with four decades of accrued interest.

But an old asset, repeated in the same way, becomes tiresome. This is what Sarah Carter’s idea of “disguised repetition” helps us to understand. The message stayed the same – “get out of the house and play” – but the outfit changed. The recipient, the line and the context all changed, while retaining the familiar feel that allows the brain to recognise the origin.

The results are evident across all the metrics, but Brand Fluency is particularly noteworthy at 95%, meaning only one in 20 viewers failed to correctly identify Caloi as the advertised brand. Our report always highlights the Distinctive Brand Assets identified by consumers, and here, the setting, logo and style were recognised as especially distinctive. The dominant spontaneous associations were “Bicycle”, “Childhood” and “Nostalgia”. The old memory became a code for instant recognition.

People are moved by bonds, which are generated by memory, which in turn is generated by emotion.

For those who lead brands, memory is a financial asset, and the brand is the manager of that portfolio. Every old campaign is a bond in the portfolio, with accumulated value in people’s minds.

Again, this is not about falling into nostalgia-core. It is about asking: what memories of my brand already exist in people’s minds, and am I treating them as heritage or as clutter?

Not every brand will have a campaign from the 1970s, 1980s or 1990s to pay tribute to. But every brand has assets, characters, phrases, slogans and images that someone, at some point, once loved. Many of those consumers are now adults with purchasing power and… fond memories.

Nostalgia takes people back to a time when their decisions were based less on price and more on feeling. Caloi looked to its legacy, remembered those who once loved it and asked them to pass that love on. What looked like a glance backwards was, in fact, a decision aimed at the brand’s future – and something almost impossible to copy.

"Childhood has changed, but some things remain essential. Playing, exploring, meeting friends, feeling the freedom of riding a bike and discovering the world beyond screens are experiences that belong to a childhood worth living. Caloi has accompanied generations of Brazilians and, with this new campaign, we want to invite parents to rediscover a little of their own childhood and give their children those same experiences. 'Don't forget your child's Caloi' is more than a campaign: it is an invitation for families to choose to spend more moments together, outdoors and on the move."

Ana Paula Nogueira Senior Marketing and Trade Manager at Caloi

“The data from System1 confirms what our intuition told us: the emotional connection of this classic Caloi campaign would have the power to transport those children of the 70s, 80s and 90s back to their own childhood. It was a small change in the message to connect with this target once more. In the end, emotional connection is perhaps the most effective tool for building brands and businesses.”

Filipe Cuvero CCO & Founding Partner at D'OM Soluções Improváveis

Creative & Media Partnership Director, LATAM (renata.buess@system1research.com)

Published: 26 November 2026

A Caloi Volta Aos Anos 80 Para Liberar O Poder Da Nostalgia

Caloi

Caloi. Infância - Convocação.

5.1
View in English

Não esqueça da minha… Ninguém esqueceu. 

Uma das campanhas mais emblemáticas do Brasil está de volta. 

“Não esqueça da minha Caloi” virou meme quando as redes sociais nem existiam e ficou nos trending topics por anos a fio, tornando-se um jeitinho bacana de lembrar alguém sobre qualquer coisa. 

Em outubro deste ano, a Caloi lançou um filme com a cara dos anos 80, feito de fotografias, e com um final que todo mundo que cresceu alugando VHS conhece bem, ter que rebobinar a antes de devolver. Isso num mercado em que todo mundo corre atrás do formato novo e da plataforma da vez. 

No Test Your Ad Pro, o filme alcançou 79% de felicidade, contra uma média brasileira de 53%. A intensidade emocional foi de 2,49, contra 1,96 da norma. A nota foi de 5,1 Estrelas, o que indica potencial de crescimento de longo prazo, e o Spike e a Fluência de Marca também ficaram em nível excepcional. Uma tríplice coroa rara.

Clique aqui para ver o relatório completo

Um que olha para trás venceu em todas as frentes, numa indústria muitas vezes obstinada em olhar para o futuro, como uma espécie de culto. O mundo da publicidade é obcecado por novidade: novas campanhas, novos posicionamentos e novas plataformas. Mas, muitas vezes, a publicidade mais eficaz surge quando as marcas olham para o seu legado de campanhas e ativos de marca e retomam sucessos anteriores. Com frequência, isso envolve reinventá-los de novas maneiras. 

Quando o psicólogo Daniel Kahneman venceu o Nobel de Economia, trouxe evidências de que, quanto mais a gente sente, mais a gente compra. Esse mote foi e ainda é utilizado pelas agências e marcas mais eficazes. A gente sabe que emoção vende e que a nostalgia é um veículo. Mas o nostalgia-core não é para todo mundo. 

E a criança dos anos 80, que hoje tem seus 45 anos, era quem queria sair de casa e pedalar, sentir o vento no cabelo, encontrar os amigos e partir para a aventura. 

Quarenta anos depois, aquelas crianças são pais e alguns até avós. E a campanha dá um passo de lado, quase imperceptível: a frase vira “Não esqueça a Caloi do seu filho”. O anúncio da Caloi agora rebobina da fita, mas fala com o adulto, e não diretamente com a criança. Isso o mantém, a princípio, fora do terreno mais sensível das regras publicitárias. É um ângulo interessante: a nostalgia como estratégia que alcança o consumo infantil passando pelo adulto que decide. A mesma mensagem muda de destinatário. A criança que pedia agora é o adulto que decide e aquela memória do consumidor deixa de ser só lembrança e vira instrução de compra para a próxima geração. 

Mas o que será que acontece dentro de quem lembra? Eu já falei disso em outra análise, mas coloco mais dados aqui, que o estrategista Richard Shotton também costuma compartilhar. Jannine Lasaleta, Constantine Sedikides e Kathleen Vohs conduziram seis experimentos publicados no Journal of Consumer Research. Participantes colocados num estado nostálgico se dispuseram a pagar mais por produtos, desembolsaram mais dinheiro (mas não mais tempo) e deram menos valor ao dinheiro. A explicação dos autores: a nostalgia enfraquece o desejo por dinheiro porque cria uma sensação de conexão social. 

Vendo os resultados do Test Your Ad da Caloi, percebemos que a nostalgia leva as pessoas de volta a um tempo em que decidiam menos pelo preço e mais pelo sentimento. A lembrança coloca o consumidor cercado de gente querida, e na memória de quase todo mundo quem aparece é a família, os amigos, a rua e a bicicleta. Nos comentários eles falam das próprias aventuras de infância e de como as crianças de hoje precisam brincar ao ar livre. O anúncio funciona como uma porta, e cada pessoa a atravessa para chegar à sua própria história. 

Vale o cuidado de Byron Sharp: esses experimentos são laboratoriais e medem disposição a pagar, não vendas. É um mecanismo plausível e bem documentado, não uma promessa de margem. Mas, aqui no nosso teste, vemos que a Caloi pode colher bons frutos, tanto agora quanto no futuro. 

Mas aqui destaco a ideia central do estudo The Magic of Compound Creativity, da System1: criatividade não se soma, ela se acumula. Cada anúncio que usa os mesmos assets, personagens, tom e códigos herda a memória dos anteriores. A Caloi tem um ativo com quatro décadas de juros acumulados. 

Mas esse asset antigo, repetido da mesma forma, cansa. É o que a ideia de repetição disfarçada (disguised repetition), de Sarah Carter, ajuda a entender. A mensagem ficou, o “saia de casa e brinque”, e a roupa mudou: mudaram o destinatário, a frase e o contexto, mantendo a pegada que faz o cérebro reconhecer a origem. 

O resultado aparece em todas as métricas, mas aqui vemos que a fluência de marca é de 95%, ou seja, só 1 em cada 20 espectadores não percebeu que o anúncio é da Caloi. Nosso relatório sempre aponta os Distinctive Brand Assets identificados pelos consumidores e, aqui, cenário, logotipo e estilo foram reconhecidos como especialmente distintivos. As mensagens espontâneas dominantes foram “Bicicleta”, “Infância” e “Nostalgia”. A memória antiga virou código de reconhecimento imediato. 

As pessoas se movem pelo vínculo, que é gerado pela memória, que é gerada pela emoção Para quem lidera marcas: a memória é um ativo financeiro, e a marca é a gestora desse portfólio. Cada campanha antiga é um título em carteira, com valor acumulado na cabeça das pessoas. 

Novamente, não é para cair no nostalgia-core. Mas perguntar: que memórias sobre a minha marca já existem na cabeça das pessoas, e eu estou tratando isso como patrimônio ou como entulho? 

Nem toda marca terá uma campanha dos anos 70, 80, 90 para homenagear. Mas toda marca tem assets, personagens, frases, slogans, imagens que alguém, em algum momento, já amou. Muitos desses consumidores hoje são adultos com poder de compra e… boas lembranças.

A nostalgia leva as pessoas de volta a um tempo em que decidiam menos pelo preço e mais pelo sentimento. A Caloi olhou para o seu legado, lembrou de quem já a amava e pediu que passasse esse amor adiante. E o que parecia olhar para trás era, na verdade, uma decisão voltada ao futuro da marca e algo quase impossível de copiar. 

“A infância mudou, mas algumas coisas continuam essenciais. Brincar, explorar, encontrar os amigos, sentir a liberdade de pedalar e descobrir o mundo fora das telas são experiências que fazem parte de uma infância que merece ser vivida. A Caloi acompanha gerações de brasileiros e, com essa nova campanha, queremos convidar os pais a resgatarem um pouco da própria infância e proporcionarem aos seus filhos essas mesmas experiências. ‘Não esqueça a Caloi do seu filho’ é mais do que uma campanha: é um convite para que as famílias escolham viver mais momentos juntos, ao ar livre e em movimento.”

Ana Paula Nogueira Gerente Sênior de Marketing e Trade da Caloi

“Os dados mostrados pela System1 comprovam o que a nossa intuição nos dizia: a conexão emocional dessa clássica campanha de Caloi teria o poder de transportar essas crianças dos anos 70, 80 e 90 para a infância delas. Foi uma pequena mudança na mensagem para se conectar com esse target outra vez. Enfim, a conexão emocional é, talvez, a ferramenta mais eficaz para se construir marcas e negócios.”

Filipe Cuvero CCO & Sócio Fundador da D’OM Soluções Improváveis

Published: 25 November 2026

From Necessity to Identity: Nine Decades of Household, Cosmetics and Personal Care

This third instalment of our journey through the history of the products that launched the brands we know and love, in collaboration with the History of Advertising Trust (HAT), brings us to household, cosmetics and personal care. Open any bathroom cabinet or cleaning cupboard and you’ll find decades of brand history sitting on the shelf. But in a category that gets more crowded every year, the brands that have lasted aren’t the ones that stood still. They kept up with the times, innovating the product, changing the way they advertised it, or both, while holding on to something that was unmistakably theirs.

The decades tell this story in three chapters. From the 1930s to the 1950s, new products solved everyday needs, and as rivals arrived, brands had to work harder to be remembered. In the 1960s and 70s, changing social attitudes, especially among young people, made products a way to express yourself. And from the 1980s, categories opened to wider audiences, and brands found new ways to talk to them. Not all innovation has to be a breakthrough, and these brands show just that. Most new products are line extensions: a new format or formula developed by an existing brand, and this blog unpacks how brands evolve naturally with societal changes. So, without further ado, let’s take a look at the brands that managed to adapt and evolve with social shifts over time – starting in the 1930s.

1930s: Innovations that revolutionised personal care and hygiene

With so many personal care products on shelves today, it’s easy to take basic hygiene for granted. But in 1933, a household antiseptic was a new idea. Dettol was developed by Reckitt & Sons in Hull and first introduced for doctors, to disinfect medical equipment, at a time when many new mothers were dying of sepsis after childbirth. Hospital trials in London reported that cases of the infection fell by more than half, and with that medical backing Dettol moved into pharmacies and, in time, into the family home. The advert below shows how Dettol positioned itself around credibility, with language such as “the modern antiseptic” that is “dangerous only to germs”. Dettol built its brand identity around being an effective, trusted item to own with everyday uses. The innovation gave Dettol its credibility, while the advertising is what carried that trust from the hospital ward to the bathroom cabinet.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

Tampax was another first. As the first commercial tampon brand, it offered something quite different from the bulkier products of the time. The design was patented by Dr Earle Haas, and it was businesswoman Gertrude Tenderich who bought the rights and built Tampax into a company, championing advertising for a product that wasn’t widely discussed in public. That early advertising was often informative: “worn internally” told women exactly what was new. Those slogans may have changed over time, but the message hasn’t. Initially advertised as less bulky and more discrete than alternative options – as seen in the “no belts, no pins, no pads” slogan below – Tampax is selling the concept of feeling comfortable and free on your period. Fast forward to today, and the “Tampax Saved My Vibe” campaign, which reworks a classic dance track, puts confidence and freedom front and centre. From providing discretion to providing confidence, what remains at the core of the brand is helping women feel good about their periods.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

Both Dettol and Tampax are brilliant examples of how innovation based on the consumer’s need can completely shape a category – they are rare breakthrough innovations. Products like these will always be necessary, but their advertising and core messages enhance the product so that the brand feels bigger than just its function.

1940s: The Origins of Andrex

Andrex toilet tissue was launched in the UK in 1942, and a decade later, the 1952 advert below shows how the brand was selling itself: a little girl cuddling a kitten, beneath a headline that says it all – ‘So very, very soft’. Here, the cuddly kitten is the imagery for softness and gentleness.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

The puppy didn’t arrive until 1972, created with agency J Walter Thompson (JWT). It’s easy to see why it worked: like the kitten in 1952, a puppy is soft, warm and cuddly, so it communicates the brand’s core promise of softness without a word. Brands live as memories in people’s heads, and the idea from the 1950s had simply found its most memorable form: the Andrex puppy that we still know and love today.

1950s: The detergent decade and standing out from the crowd

If Andrex shows how one brand can become memorable, the 1950s show what happens when lots of brands try to do it at once. Wash day was changing. For generations it had meant boiling whites in a copper and rubbing stains by hand, but electric washing machines were finding their way into more homes – the first automatic electric washing machine appeared in 1937, and production for household use soared after the Second World War – and a wave of new detergents arrived to go with them.

Packaging, taglines, claims and mascots all helped make a product feel unique and build a brand, and each of these adverts leans on something different. Tide leads with a bold claim and the proof to back it up: the “world’s cleanest weekly wash”, guaranteed, with a cartoon of delighted neighbours and letters from customers. Surf takes a specific ritual and makes it its own, with “You need Surf for a spotless boil!” and the confident title of “the world’s most complete detergent”. Daz turns a colour into a distinctive asset: boil “the blue way”, it says. All three are built around the traditional wash day of rubbing and boiling. Fairy Snow, though, speaks to a newer kind of shopper: “Washing machine owners!”. When products are this similar, the brand does the work the product can’t. What gets remembered at the shelf is the name, the colour, the character or the line.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

Look closely at all four adverts and you’ll spot something else they share: the woman doing the washing, whether she’s hanging out sheets, carrying the laundry basket or pouring powder into the boiler. That reflects who handled most of the household washing and shopping at the time, and the brands spoke to her directly. It’s a detail worth remembering, because by the 1960s a new generation of shoppers was about to change the conversation.

1960s: Shifting attitudes, cosmetic trends and self-expression

The 1960s brought an attitude shift, centred on youth, that reshaped the cosmetics industry. It was felt strongly in London, where fashion and music were moving so quickly that culture seemed to relax almost overnight, and with it, advertising. Fashion led the way, with Mary Quant popularising the mini skirt and putting bold colour and youthful designs at the centre of London style. The same shift is visible in music, with the neat matching suits on The Beatles’ record covers in 1963 evolving into the psychedelic colour of Sgt. Pepper in 1967.

Behind this shift was the post-war baby boom, which had created a large and influential group of teenagers and young women. Alongside second-wave feminism and increased female employment, this helped position make-up as a tool for personal expression, rather than something young women adopted to follow their mothers’ lead. The Twiggy era brought a new gamine, androgynous ideal in which the eyes took centre stage, through dark liners, shadows and false lashes. Colourful, playful, affordable make-up replaced the idea of cosmetics as a daily ritual with a younger, trendier view: a look could be new and change every day. As the creative revolution made its way over from the US, brands started speaking to their audiences in bolder and more playful ways.

Boots No7 was already a familiar name by then. Launched in 1935 as a skincare range, with colour cosmetics added in 1937, it was well placed for the colour boom: an accessible high-street brand for the growing number of young women with some disposable income. The idea of make-up as changeable and colourful suited an affordable brand, because customers could buy different shades of the same products and join in with the trends. The No7 advert below dates from 1958, right on the turn of the decade, so it shows the starting line rather than the full 1960s look. The imagery is still polished, with a wide-brimmed hat and a bold pink lip, and the lipstick is pitched at “a girl who loves her lips”. But the seeds are there: the ad promises “a galaxy of gorgeous colours”. Choice, colour and affordability were exactly what the next generation would be looking for. In many ways this attitude continues in cosmetics today, as make-up has become a form of expression more than ever, and No7 has held its position as an affordable, trusted high-street brand.

Max Factor’s identity, on the other hand, had been built around film studios, Hollywood glamour and the polished looks of the 1940s and 50s. To stay relevant, it stretched beyond colour cosmetics and spoke in a younger voice. This 1964 advert is for a perfumed spray deodorant, a natural line extension from make-up into everyday personal care. The model’s tousled hair, direct and youthful gaze and bold, defined eye makes her look playful and confident rather than studio-polished, which leans into that 1960s attitude.

Elizabeth Arden, a brand built around ladylike luxury, shows a similar adaptation. The illustration of the “Sea Orchid” ad shows two women with pale pink and bright blue eyeshadow, dark liner and long lashes, wearing soft coral-pink lips rather than a bold red. The eyes take centre stage, exactly the look defining the decade, and luxury hasn’t gone away, it simply comes in a more colourful, more modern form. Not every brand can lead the charge when social shifts change demand, but they can adapt, through innovation, advertising or both, to stay relevant.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

Colour wasn’t confined to the make-up bag. The mood of the decade reached even everyday household products, and nowhere is that clearer than in the Brillo advert below. A bright pink soap pad, a pack in bold primary colours and a pan with a smile drawn on it: “Bring back the smile with Brillo”. The idea is simple and memorable. The smile is the proof that the pan is clean, and it puts a feeling at the heart of what could have been a very functional advert for scouring pads.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

1970s: Confidence in a can

By the 1970s, the deodorant aisle was a busy place, and Sure’s advert shows how a brand could stand out with a clear promise and a pack that did the talking. “New unbeatable Sure!” the headline announces, offering a “promise of confidence” that no rival can match. What’s striking is what the advert leaves out: there’s no model and no scene, just the cans themselves and a single hand reaching in. Seen one way, it’s a confident move: the pack is the hero, and the product is left to speak for itself. Seen another, it keeps the promise open to everyone, because with nobody pictured, the advert sells confidence as a feeling to have rather than a type of person to be, which reflects the changes in social attitudes at the time.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

 

1980s: New audiences, new positioning

By the 1980s, the market for personal care was widening. Timotei arrived in the UK in 1983 with a promise that was simple and memorable: a shampoo “so mild you can wash your hair as often as you like”. The claim was backed by a gentle formulation with natural herb extracts, but it was the world around it that people remembered: a woman in a white dress, a basket of wildflowers and a summer meadow, with a scent to match. The gentle formulation of the product combined with advertising full of nature and natural beauty worked harmoniously together, and the brand grew into a conditioner and skincare range, proving that when the advertising matches the product, a brand identity is formed.

Lynx took a different route. Launched in the UK in 1985 after debuting in France as Axe in 1983, it was a stand-alone body spray created for young men, and it made fragrance part of the daily routine. A new product format opened up a new category, and the brand soon built a range around it. The advert below is for Lynx aftershave, a classic line extension of the same brand and attitude, for a new use.

The advertising does the rest. Set in a crowded, black-and-white party, with a young man noticed across the room, the line “Because first impressions last” turns fragrance from a grooming step into a social confidence booster, giving the product a clear promise of confidence and attraction. Together, the product and the advertising opened the personal care industry up to men, making it feel like a natural part of life for young men.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

1990s:

By the 1990s, Nivea was already a household name, but this advert shows it doing something new. Nivea Creme, launched in 1911, is known for its rich formula and blue tin. Nivea Soft arrived in 1994 as a lighter, quick-absorbing moisturiser for the face, body and hands, and its advertising is built around that lightness. The ad below, from 1997, promises “a new softness for my skin instantly” and invites you to “enjoy the sensation of summer rain on your skin”. This sensory promise expresses the light, fast-absorbing formula as a feeling you can imagine. The pack changed too, from the blue tin to a white tub, reflecting the lightness of the product.

This makes Nivea a great case study for developing new products that align with the brand. This is a textbook line extension, as Nivea Soft grew from Nivea Creme rather than replacing it, to answer a slight shift in demand. The name, the trusted heritage and the familiar colours stayed constant, so the brand remained instantly recognisable, while the new product met demand for lighter, softer skincare. It’s a great example of fluent innovation: the principle whereby ideas are easier to buy if they skew towards something we already know and love, rather than shock us. Too much surprise can present a “risk” to customers, so fluent innovations tend to balance happiness with surprise by the ratio of 80:20.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

2000s: Selling an icon

In 2005, David Beckham launched his first fragrance, Instinct, with fragrance company Coty, and went on to sell more than ten million bottles by its tenth anniversary. If Lynx made fragrance part of a young man’s routine in the 1980s, Instinct shows how far men’s grooming had come twenty years later: stylish, aspirational and personal. The advert below keeps things simple: Beckham in a dark jacket with his shirt open against a brooding sky, a bottle carrying his name, and just a few quiet words announcing “the new fragrance for men”.

Beckham shows just how far brands had embedded themselves in culture. By the 2000s, televised sport, music television and booming celebrity press put stars in living rooms every day, making pop culture part of everyday life like it had never been before. Brands quickly learned to draw on this, and created their own pop revolution in advertising, by placing the product into a world people were already watching. Beckham isn’t a mascot in the Andrex sense. He’s the face of the product, and a role model. Having one of the world’s best-known sportsmen put his name and image to a fragrance helped make grooming feel mainstream and aspirational for men, giving them permission to care about how they look and smell.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

Create with Confidence®

From Dettol’s hospital trials to Beckham’s Instinct, these brands have one thing in common: each changed something and kept something. Products, slogans and audiences may shift and change to reflect the times, but the brands core messaging stayed recognisable. As more products entered the market, those brands were the ones that stayed relevant, because strong branding meant people still knew them when everything around them changed.

So, if you’re ready to create the next product or campaign that stands the test of time – whether it’s a breakthrough innovation or a natural line extension – System1 can help. Is Texture the Next Big Food Trend? What October’s Top Innovations Reveal

How do you spot the next big food trend before it reaches peak popularity? And, just as importantly, how do you know when a trend has run its course? From pistachio and matcha to protein and, more recently, fiber, the food and beverage landscape is constantly evolving. But for FMCG brands, success isn’t simply about jumping on the latest bandwagon. It’s about understanding what is driving consumer demand and finding new ways to translate those preferences into meaningful product differentiation.

And those opportunities don’t always come down to flavor. Texture, format, and unexpected product combinations can be just as powerful in capturing consumer attention and creating new occasions for familiar favorites. October’s top US innovations offered an interesting case in point, with crispy emerging as a recurring theme across the category. From new cookie innovations and chocolate-biscuit collaborations to a Twix frosted cookie and crunchy New York bakery bites, brands are finding fresh ways to reinvent familiar treats through texture.

At System1, we test the latest innovations hitting the market every week through Test Your Innovation, giving us a live view of how consumer preferences and emerging trends are taking shape. Recently, we’ve seen growing demand for functional fiber benefits, while in chocolate and confectionery, texture is proving to be another compelling route to differentiation.

But how can brands identify the next opportunity before investing in development and taking it to market? That’s where testing comes in. Test Your Innovation helps brands evaluate everything from product names and claims to flavors and full concepts, putting ideas in front of real consumers before significant investment is made. By testing different combinations, positioning, and sensory cues, marketers can understand what’s resonating, identify opportunities to optimize, and spot the concepts with the greatest potential to stand out on shelf.

The ambition? To find the next Nerds Gummy Clusters, not simply follow the trend, but get ahead of it.

Finding the Next Star Idea

So, how can brands separate the next big opportunity from the ideas that simply follow the crowd? Test Your Innovation gives every concept a clear, comparable measure of success: the Star Rating.

Scored on a scale of 1.0 to 5.9, the Star Rating helps brands understand an idea’s potential before it reaches the shelf. And the commercial opportunity is significant: 5 Star ideas have 3x the sales potential of 1 Star ideas.

But the score is only part of the story. Each Test Your Innovation report provides deeper diagnostics, from implicit brand associations and usage occasions to demographic appeal and actionable recommendations for improving an idea.

The Star Rating itself combines three key measures: emotional appeal, whether consumers would buy or sell shares in the idea and their decision speed. Emotional response is one of the strongest predictors of consumer behavior, revealing how an idea makes people feel rather than relying solely on what they say they might buy. Share trading adds another layer, while decision speed helps measure how easily consumers understand and connect with the concept.

That last element matters. Ideas that are immediately understood and accepted by consumers are more fluent, making them easier to process, more familiar and ultimately more likely to succeed. By bringing these three measures together, the Star Rating gives brands a robust view of innovation potential, helping them identify the ideas worth backing, the ones that need refining and the opportunities that could become tomorrow’s category stars.

Let’s take a closer look at October’s top innovations, what they reveal about the evolving tastes and preferences of US consumers, and the opportunities they could signal for the future of food and beverage.

October’s Top Innovations

1. Ghirardelli Cripsy Cookies – 5.9 Stars

2. King’s Hawaiian Maple Rolls – 5.8 Stars

 

3. Toblerone x Biscoff Truffles – 5.7 Stars

4. Ritter Sport Duos – 5.3 Stars

5. Twix Frosted Cookie – 5.1 Stars

6. Tootsie Roll Hoots – 4.6 Stars

7. Kraft String Cheese – 4.6 Stars

8. New York Bakery Bites – 4.6 Stars

9. Tru Fru Cherry Truffles – 4.2 Stars

10. Oh Goody! Protein Gummy Cubes – 3.9 Stars

Will Premium Indulgence Win in the GLP-1 Era?

Three clear signals emerged from this round of innovation testing.

Crispy is the texture consumers are talking about. “Texture” came up unprompted in consumer verbatims for Toblerone Biscoff Truffles, Ghirardelli and Ritter Sport Duos. Crispy and crunchy textures are emerging as a real driver of appeal, and NPD teams should build it into concepts early rather than treat it as a late-stage detail.

Sweet still dominates. Sugary products took almost every position in the top ten. The only savory entries were New York bakery’s cheese bites and Kraft’s new grab-and-go string cheese.

Premium is where the momentum is. Toblerone Biscoff Truffles, Tru Fru cherries, Ghirardelli cookies and Ritter Sport are not everyday treats. They sit at the pricier end of the shelf, and consumers are responding to them.

So where does GLP-1 fit in? With so much industry focus on GLP-1 and changing eating habits, these results suggest we may be early in writing off indulgence. Consumers still want a treat. What may be shifting is how they choose one. Rather than suppressing the sweet tooth, GLP-1 and wider health awareness could be making shoppers more selective, favoring a fix that feels worthwhile over a quick one. For NPD and insight teams, the question becomes less “should we launch indulgent products?” and more “is our indulgence worth it, on price, on quality and on experience?”

With results validated against real in-market sales, you’re not just finding out whether people like your idea. You’re finding out whether it has what it takes to grow your brand.

Crispy Cookies

Want to stay ahead of the latest winning innovation trends? Innovation of the Week, powered by System1’s Test Your Innovation testing, is your regular spotlight on the newest concepts hitting the market. 

Speak to our innovation team today!

A reputation for quality is one of the most valuable assets a brand can have when it’s looking to introduce a new product or expand into a new category. But a brand’s premium status is like a Ming vase – you need to be very careful transferring it. Get a launch wrong and the blowback can dilute or even damage your brand’s hard-won status. Get it right and you have a winner.

Premium chocolate brand Ghirardelli gets it absolutely right with this week’s Innovation Of The Week, their Crispy Cookies product, which gets a very rare maximum 5.9-Stars on our Test Your Innovation.

A Test Your Innovation Star Rating is built from a combination of factors – the type of emotional response to a product, the “share trading game” where people choose whether or not they’d buy shares in the new idea, and the speed of response to that decision which shows how easy the concept is to understand.

With its elegant packaging evoking the wider Ghirardelli brand and a simple to grasp idea, the Crispy Cookies get exceptional results on all three measures that go into the Star Rating score. Maybe the most impressive is the emotional response – even in a category like cookies, to make 75% of participants happy is an amazing achievement. (The US average across all tests is 38%). 81% of respondents would buy shares in the Crispy Cookies: another extremely high score.

What makes the Crispy Cookies concept so successful? To answer that we should check the Implicit Attributes results – where we ask people to rapidly associate each product with various descriptions. Ghirardelli gets above-the-norm scores across every attribute but some particularly stand out: near-maximum scores for “Believable”, “Recognisable”, “Fits With The Brand” and “High Quality”. “Exciting”, “Premium”, “Recommended” and “Trustworthy” also score above 90% each.

The overall picture is clear. Ghirardelli has successfully carried its premium reputation over to the cookie aisle, with packaging and branding that communicate quality and trust and lead to those sky high test scores. There’s no sign of the big risk for a premium innovation – lack of credibility.

There’s something else we can learn from the Implicit Attributes test, too. The one potential barrier the test identifies is price – in the “suggested improvements” comments people suggest lowering the price (without knowing what it will be!). But is this really going to be an issue? We think it won’t be, based on the very strong results for “Value For Money” and “Worth More”, high above the test norm. People are expecting a premium cookie from Ghirardelli and feel it’ll be well worth the money.

5.9-Star ideas don’t come along every day. Ghirardelli should be delighted with these results which point to a premium brand that’s expanding with exactly the right product at the right time.

We’re starting with Mastercard, who are promoting their new Mastercard Collection, a suite of benefits available to their higher-tier global members, including exclusive discounts on top hotels, travel destinations and restaurants. Their new ad “Together Is Better” boasts top-tier Brand Fluency and lands in the top 5% of the Credit Services category, testament to how well creative consistency has worked for them.

It’s been almost 30 years since Mastercard transformed credit card advertising with their Priceless campaign, the first credit card ads to move beyond features and availability and really go for the emotional benefits of membership. Priceless was a phenomenal success, growing Mastercard’s market share, and the insights that drive it are still relevant today.

At the heart of the campaign is the idea that Mastercard offers its customers the freedom to experience moments that are truly precious, and that’s as powerful a selling point now as it was in 1997. The new ad still uses “Priceless” as its tagline.

“Together Is Better” presents that insight in a relaxing, unhurried way, with an unusual collage technique switching between stills and video as a voiceover describes how a pair of siblings fly out to New York for a reunion with their sister, who’s built a career and an adult life there. It takes no time at all for the three of them to be back laughing together like they did as kids – and it’s the Mastercard Collection that allowed these moments of family joy to happen.

While Priceless opened the door to more emotional ads in the Credit Services category, other brands have not always taken advantage. The sector as a whole still has only a 1.9-Star Rating average, meaning that most Credit Services ads are simply not a good brand growth investment.

Mastercard’s ad scores 3.5-Stars, a good score in any category but in the top 5% of this underperforming sector. It’s also Mastercard’s best performing ad in the last 4 years, showing how strongly the “Priceless” idea still resonates when matched to an emotional story. Short-term Spike Rating, and Emotional Intensity, are also good scores and both are way over the category average.

In the Test Your Ad report we can also break down the key moments in the ad – its peak of Happiness in the closing shot of the family united around a dining table at 49s, and the early spike in Fluency as the collage section makes sure to show the Mastercard logo prominently.

In fact it’s Brand Fluency where the ad really stands out, with a huge 96% recognition putting “Together Is Better” in the top 2% of ads in the Credit Services category, and making it Mastercard’s most fluent ad of the decade.

It’s not hard to see where this strong branding comes from. There’s discreet use of the logos and branding all through the ad, but the emotional peak comes when the voiceover drops the “Priceless” tagline at the end. It’s not just that the insight remains strong after three decades, it’s that consistent use of the same creative idea has generated enormous brand recognition and cultural footprint. When you have an ad which uses that well – and “Together Is Better” certainly does – it’s a recipe for effectiveness. Creative consistency really is priceless.

From household names to own-label challengers: Why brands can’t afford to stand still

As we continue our journey through the history of the products that launched the brands we know and love today, in collaboration with the History of Advertising Trust, we’re turning our attention to tea, coffee and biscuits. A category that has evolved from everyday convenience to premium experiences at home, and one built on the foundations of some of Britain’s most enduring household names, from Tetley and Twinings to Nescafé.

As with our previous exploration of confectionery, we’ll be travelling decade by decade, revisiting the products, campaigns and innovations that helped shape the category. But this time, there’s a bigger question at the heart of the story: what happens when the brands that once led innovation are no longer the ones setting the pace?

The balance of power in food and drink has shifted considerably. Branded products accounted for 82% of all new food and drink launches in 2000. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 47%, with own label now accounting for the majority at 53%.

It’s a telling sign of how much the landscape has changed. Retailers are increasingly taking the lead in product innovation, giving consumers more choice and challenging established brands to work harder to earn their place on the shelf. Familiarity alone is no longer enough. Brands need to keep giving people reasons to choose them, remember them and, crucially, seek them out by name.

That’s why continuous innovation matters. It’s not simply about launching something new for the sake of it. It’s about keeping a brand distinctive, relevant and desirable, creating products that offer genuine value while building on the character and associations that make the brand worth choosing in the first place. And when paired with effective advertising, innovation becomes even more powerful: giving brands something meaningful to say, creating consumer demand and helping them command a premium beyond the product’s functional benefits.

And it’s not only consumers who notice. With own label now accounting for the majority of new launches, retailers are both a brand’s competitor and its gatekeeper. Brands that consistently bring genuinely new ideas to the category, the kind that draw shoppers in and grow the category as a whole, give retailers a reason to stock them, support them and make room for them on the shelf. Innovation sets a brand apart from its competitors in the eyes of the retailer, not just the consumer.

So, as we wind back the clock to the 1940s, we’ll explore how tea, coffee and biscuits have evolved, the innovations that changed the category and the advertising that helped turn everyday products into household names. Because if there’s one thing this history demonstrates, it’s that the brands we remember are rarely the ones that stood still.

1940s: How Nescafé made instant coffee a household name

The stereotype is true: Britain is a nation of tea lovers. A staple of everyday life, tea was the nation’s preferred hot drink throughout both World Wars. But with tea rationed for 12 years between 1940 and 1952, there was an opportunity for another drink to take centre stage: coffee.

Today, Nescafé is a household name, but in the 1940s, it was still establishing itself. Following a surplus of coffee beans in Brazil, Nestlé set out to develop a soluble coffee that could reduce waste while delivering a convenient, great-tasting product. Swiss chemist Max Morgenthaler led the product development, spending seven years perfecting a way to bring instant coffee to life. First launched in Switzerland in 1938, Nescafé had reached more than 30 countries by 1940, even becoming part of US soldiers’ emergency rations during the Second World War.

Nor was Nescafé the first attempt at making coffee quick and easy at home. Since the late 19th century, British households had been able to reach for Camp Coffee, a Glasgow-made liquid essence stirred into hot water or milk. But with sugar and chicory doing most of the work, and only a small proportion of actual coffee, its taste was, to put it kindly, an acquired one. Camp lives on today, though it’s more at home in the baking aisle than in the cup. Nescafé promised something much closer to a proper cup of coffee, with the same convenience.

But winning over Britain’s tea drinkers required more than an innovative product. Nescafé’s early advertising encouraged trial through free samples, emphasising convenience and great taste. Familiar imagery, including coffee served in traditional teacups, helped make this new product feel less unfamiliar. It was a clever way to introduce a new drinking habit without asking consumers to abandon the rituals they already loved.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

The takeaway? Fluent Innovation in action. Nescafé introduced a completely new product format, but surrounded it with familiar cues. By making coffee look, feel and fit into everyday life much like tea, it offered consumers something new without making the choice feel like a significant leap. This is the principle of Fluent Innovation: 80% familiar, 20% new. When innovation builds on what consumers already recognise and love, the perceived trade-off and risk of trying something different are reduced, making the decision to choose it that much easier.

1950s: Maxwell House brings a little fun to the coffee aisle

By the 1950s, the UK coffee market was attracting challengers, and Nescafé was no longer without competition. Enter Maxwell House, the Tennessee-born coffee brand setting its sights on the market leader.

Its approach? A little more fun. For its 1959 UK television launch, Maxwell House introduced a catchy jingle and showcased its coffee in jars, using entertainment and showmanship to capture attention. While Nescafé had established convenience and ease as key selling points, Maxwell House added something more: personality, distinctive branding and a reason to remember it.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

It’s an approach that continues to work today. The strongest brands don’t just create memorable individual campaigns; they build coherent creative platforms that give consumers something recognisable to return to, year after year.

Take Yorkshire Tea, for example. Having challenged an established tea market, the brand has built a distinctive identity around its ‘Where Everything’s Done Proper’ platform. Its advertising repeatedly takes increasingly ridiculous and entertaining approaches to demonstrate just how far the brand will go to deliver the perfect cup of tea. Different campaigns, same recognisable brand character.

While Maxwell House’s approach was perhaps less developed, the foundations were already there. In just one decade, coffee advertising was moving beyond functional product benefits towards entertainment, brand personality and distinctive creative ideas. A shift that would come to define modern brand building.

But how did Nescafé respond to the growing competition? Let’s turn to the 1960s.

1960s: When innovation becomes the category standard

By the 1960s, Nescafé had a new challenge. Competitors weren’t just entering the market; they were beginning to outpace the brand in areas such as packaging. Maxwell House had introduced coffee in glass jars, giving its product a more premium feel, while Nescafé was still largely associated with its traditional tins. It was a reminder that innovation isn’t just about what’s inside the pack. How a product looks and feels can be just as important in shaping perceptions of quality.

Nescafé needed to respond. In 1965, it introduced Nescafé Gold Blend, bringing coffee to consumers in glass jars and positioning the product around premium quality, freshness and great taste. Its advertising reinforced this proposition through product demonstrations, highlighting the freshness and ease of preparation while building on the brand’s established reputation for great-tasting coffee.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

But here’s where the story gets interesting. Nearly 70 years later, the coffee aisle still looks remarkably familiar. Glass jars remain a dominant format, with own-label competitors offering products that look strikingly similar to the established brands they sit alongside. An innovation that once helped Nescafé stand apart has, over time, become a category convention.

The takeaway? Innovation can give brands a competitive advantage, but that advantage doesn’t last forever. When competitors replicate your packaging, product formats or points of difference, what once made you distinctive can quickly become the norm. And as own label continues to challenge established brands, there’s a bigger question to ask: are brands still leading the category, or simply defending the position they’ve already built? Continuous innovation is what keeps brands moving forwards, rather than allowing yesterday’s breakthrough to become tomorrow’s standard.

1970s: Coffee culture evolves, but where is the innovation?

By the 1960s, coffee had become about more than what was in the jar. Britain’s espresso bar boom had brought a new social dimension to the category, with Soho’s Italian-style coffee bars becoming popular hangouts for young people, music lovers and the emerging youth culture. But by the middle of the decade, many of these independent coffee bars were beginning to disappear, giving way to more conventional cafés and restaurants.

Meanwhile, at home, coffee was becoming an increasingly familiar part of everyday life. The market was also seeing the emergence of new branded products beyond coffee itself. In 1967, Mr Kipling launched its range of packaged cakes, bringing branded indulgence into the everyday tea and coffee occasion. By the end of the 1970s, it had become the UK’s number one cake brand.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

Then came another name that would go on to reshape Britain’s coffee culture. In 1971, Italian brothers Sergio and Bruno Costa established a London coffee roastery, developing their now-famous Mocha Italia blend. Initially supplying coffee to hotels and other establishments, the business wouldn’t open its first coffee shop until 1981.

Yet, despite these cultural shifts, the packaged coffee market was beginning to look somewhat familiar. Instant coffee remained a convenient household staple, while the excitement around coffee was increasingly moving towards the experience of drinking it out of home. Brands were no longer simply competing with one another on the supermarket shelf; they were competing with the atmosphere, authenticity and experience of independent coffee houses.

Consumer habits don’t stand still, and neither should brands. As coffee moved from the kitchen cupboard into cafés and social spaces, the occasions, expectations and experiences surrounding the category changed. The challenge for established brands was to keep pace with those changes, finding new ways to remain relevant rather than relying on the familiarity of products consumers already knew.

1980s: One nibble and you’re nobbled

While coffee brands were navigating changing consumption habits, the 1980s brought us back to another familiar British ritual: tea and biscuits. And it was here that McVitie’s spotted an opportunity to innovate without asking consumers to change their habits.

In 1985, McVitie’s launched Hobnobs, an oaty, crunchy alternative to the traditional digestive, designed with dunking firmly in mind. Its television launch introduced the now-iconic line, “One Nibble and You’re Nobbled”, using humour and a memorable name to give this new biscuit an identity of its own.

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

The advertising cleverly balanced familiarity with novelty. McVitie’s drew on the trust and heritage of its established biscuit range, including Digestives and Rich Teas, while introducing something a little different. The familiar tea-time occasion remained, but the product offered a new texture, taste and personality. Consumers didn’t have to rethink their biscuit habits; they simply had another reason to reach for the packet.

And the innovation didn’t stop there. Following the success of the original, McVitie’s introduced milk and dark chocolate varieties in 1987, extending the range while building on a product consumers already loved.

Hobnobs are a brilliant example of Fluent Innovation: 80% familiar, 20% new. A trusted brand, a familiar biscuit format and an established tea-time ritual, with just enough novelty to spark interest and encourage trial. By making the new feel recognisable, McVitie’s reduced the perceived risk of trying something different, while distinctive naming and entertaining advertising gave consumers something memorable to associate with the brand.

And unlike the coffee aisle, where some of the same product formats and packaging have endured for decades, the biscuit category continued to demonstrate how established brands could find fresh ways to innovate around familiar favourites.

1990s: Have we reached the limits of instant coffee innovation?

Our final stop on this journey through the tea, coffee and biscuit products that helped build the brands we know and love takes us to the 1990s, and the launch of Brooke Bond’s Café Mountain. The same Brooke Bond behind PG Tips, which had helped shape Britain’s tea-drinking habits since the 1930s.

Café Mountain arrived with a distinctive advertising campaign and a fresh positioning, but the product itself felt remarkably familiar. The packaging, format and overall proposition followed conventions that had been established decades earlier. The brand had found a new way to market coffee, but had it really found a new way to innovate?

Source: The History of Advertising Trust

Fast forward to today, and instant coffee is available in all shapes and forms, from flavoured varieties to ready-made cappuccino sachets. Some more recent launches have certainly pushed the boundaries, including M&S’s flavoured instant coffee offerings, with popcorn and caramel among the more unusual flavour combinations. But when it comes to the fundamentals of instant coffee, how much has really changed since Nescafé first brought it to market in the 1930s?

Perhaps that’s the bigger question for established brands. The products, packaging and positioning that once made them distinctive have become familiar category conventions. And as own label continues to grow, retailers can draw on many of those same conventions to create products that look and feel remarkably similar, often competing on price.

Even the category’s biggest revolution hasn’t been immune. In 1986, Nestlé, the company behind Nescafé, looked beyond the jar altogether and launched Nespresso: a capsule system that brought café-style espresso into the home and turned coffee from an everyday convenience into a premium experience. Backed by glossy advertising fronted by George Clooney, it showed that consumers would happily pay more for coffee that felt genuinely new. But when Nespresso’s patents began to expire in 2012, compatible capsules soon followed, including supermarket own-label versions sitting on the very same shelves. Innovation can redefine a category, but it takes continuous innovation to keep leading it.

Create with Confidence®

The history of tea, coffee and biscuits shows us just how powerful innovation can be in building brands, creating new habits and establishing products that stand the test of time. But it also highlights the danger of standing still. The very products and conventions that helped build today’s household names have also shaped the own-label ranges now challenging them on supermarket shelves.

From Nescafé making instant coffee familiar in the 1940s, to Maxwell House bringing entertainment into coffee advertising, Gold Blend creating a premium proposition, Hobnobs reinventing the familiar biscuit occasion and Nespresso bringing the coffee shop home, one thing is clear: brands need both advertising and innovation to keep moving forwards.

Today’s Innovation Of The Week is a brand extension that represents a big step between channels for restaurant brand Toby Carvery. They’re moving into the retail space for the first time with a selection of frozen ready meals which were an exclusive September launch in frozen food retailers Iceland and Food Warehouse. As usual, our Test Your Innovation report gives a snapshot of the strengths, potential market and possible barriers for the new line.

A restaurant chain moving to retail makes intuitive sense but successes in this space are rarer than you’d think. It’s far from easy to recreate the taste experience loyal restaurant customers are used to at home, and if you get it wrong it can have knock-on effects on your brand perception. But if you can successfully establish an at-home extension – like Pizza Express’ range of chilled supermarket pizzas, or iced drinks from Starbucks and Costa Coffee – it raises your brand’s fluency and mental availability alongside its revenue.

Toby Carvery have gone big with this launch, offering 15 different lines to reflect the full Carvery roast dinner experience. The packaging is elegant and premium-looking while reflecting the parent brand, and the range includes full meals, sides and party bites. On our Test Your Innovation report it scores a strong 4.2-Stars, putting it above the 85th percentile of all ideas in our database.

The main driver of this is a very strong result in the “share trading game”, where we ask a panel if they’d buy shares in the idea. This measure takes us beyond personal emotional response (which is also good for Toby Carvery) and into a prediction of wider success. A strong result here shows the frozen range is an idea that feels right to consumers.

We get a further sense of that product-market fit by looking at the suggestions for improvement and the attributes test (where people rapidly associate the product with a set of keywords). In this case the attributes Toby Carvery outscores the average on are “Believable”, “Fits With The Brand” and in particular “Recognisable”. The suggestions and comments stress the importance of the Toby brand to the offer, with panelists praising the brand, the range of food on offer and feeling unable to suggest any obvious improvements.

What this tells us is that the Toby Carvery frozen range has avoided that critical issue faced by the restaurant-to-retail extension – the question of credibility. People are happy to accept that the Toby brand can work as a frozen at-home range, and plenty are actively excited by the idea.

Is there any catch? The one thing the brand should consider in its marketing is the brand’s perceived demographic profile. While it’s seen as a product that appeals to families, the report predicts Toby Carvery frozen meals will especially appeal to retirees and older people in general. That goes hand in hand with “modern” as a below-average attribute for the product and with comments suggesting that Toby meals don’t fit well with healthy eating trends.

None of that’s a criticism of the product, which we’d predict to be a success. But it’s the kind of insight that can shape the way a new idea goes to market – whether Toby Carvery lean in to this perceived older appeal or push back on it, for instance. For now, the brand has created a range that will carve a place in the competitive frozen food aisle with strong brand recognition and proven popularity.

Thatchers and Aardman Score a Christmas First

Thatchers

Saving Tasting Time this Christmas

5.9

Welcome to our new Ad Of The Month column where we dive deep on one of the month’s most interesting ads – asking what makes it effective, what our Test Your Ad diagnostics tell us about it, and what your brand can learn from it. This month it’s Thatchers Cider, with a record-breaking 5.9-Star ad, their best ever commercial and the first ever Cider Christmas ad. 

Thatchers are an unexpected newcomer in the Christmas ad race. It’s the time when brands roll out their best and biggest ads of the year, and we’re used to retailers leading the pack. But it’s not just shopping brands that can take advantage of the heightened emotions and open wallers of the festive season.  

Thatchers Cider and agency Bray Leino have come up with a charming animated Christmas adventure all about saving the brand’s famous “Tasting Time” quality check when the farm is snowed in. The maximum 5.9-Star Rating on Test Your Ad breaks all records for a Christmas drinks commercial – the category average is only 3.1-Stars. 

Long-term Star Rating isn’t the only area where “Saving Tasting Time” excels. It scores 65% Happiness (UK average 36%), an Exceptional short term Spike Rating (1.37 vs a category average of 1.18) and an Emotional Intensity of 1.73 (maximum 3, and category average only 1.31). 

To get these exceptional results, Thatchers had the best possible help. They called in Aardman Animations to create the ad, and while Thatchers may be new to the Christmas ad game, Aardman have a superb pedigree, lending classic characters like Shaun The Sheep and Wallace And Gromit to many brands over the years and always getting very strong results. Check out their 2025 Christmas ad with Barbour, a 5.8-Star festive treat. 

One of the interesting things about Aardman’s collaboration with Thatchers, though, is that the cider brand has stayed away from that kind of pre-existing character, what we at System1 call a “Hired Device”. We’ve explored how “Hired Devices” compare with Fluent Devices – recurring characters owned by the brand – and discovered that while Hired Devices often work well for a one-off, Fluent Devices are better at driving the creative consistency that leads to long-term success. 

Thatchers and Aardman have shown this by developing a true partnership. It combines the brand’s existing set of Fluent Devices and brand assets with Aardman’s world-beating animation craft and know-how. Thatchers ads were already extremely well-branded and consistent, and Aardman has helped take that to the next level. 

So this ad’s success is built on a successful existing foundation – the skill with which Thatchers has built a brand around its family business. Founder Martin Thatcher, his family, his dog, Myrtle Farm and the “Tasting Time” ritual are all lovingly recreated by Aardman (Martin’s coat alone took an entire week to make!). It’s no coincidence that the peak moment of Happiness in “Saving Tasting Time” comes when we see the whole family together at 22s. 

But these things all resonate and feel familiar to viewers because they’ve shown up over the years in other Thatchers ads. Martin Thatcher in particular stands alongside John Warburton as a brand owner who’s turned himself into a brand asset – making the brand feel authentic and personal. What Aardman did is take those existing assets and opened up their world to allow the kind of great animated storytelling you simply couldn’t do in live action.  

You can see that charm and craft at work in Aardman’s first collaboration with Thatchers, a 4.7-Star ad from 2023. All the brand assets from the Christmas ad are here, wrapped up in the message of care and perfectionism Thatchers wants to put across. One of the reasons Aardman and Thatchers are a great fit is this shared belief that craft and detail are worth caring about, and that really comes across in their ads. 

The Aardman-created Thatchers Christmas ad is a genuine first – it’s the first time any cider brand has run a Christmas ad. It moves away from the sun-soaked imagery of the typical cider ad to a wintry landscape which Aardman makes wonderfully cosy. The brand worked with System1 to test the ad and understand whether this move into unusual cider territory pays off. 

And it has paid off. Branding is strong throughout, with a particular lift when we first see Myrtle the Dog at 6 seconds. And in the key associations chart in Test Your Ad Pro, “Cider” and “Christmas” share first place. 

But to long-time watchers of Thatchers and Aardman it shouldn’t be a surprise the ad performs so well, breaking records and getting a 5-Star score across every demographic. The groundwork for its success has been carefully laid over the years by Thatchers nurturing of brand assets and Aardman’s deep understanding of advertising showmanship. The seeds for this perfect harvest were planted a long time ago. 

1 Big Lesson: Strong brand assets let you take big creative risks. Thatchers entered a category with no Christmas ad tradition and still achieved the maximum score because its familiar faces, places, and rituals were already doing the hard work.
